seg: ABSTRACT Objective: To report an association between two autoimmune conditions, Graves’ disease and stiff-person (stiff-man) syndrome, and discuss the relevant literature. Methods: We present a case of a 52-year-old white woman with stiff-person syndrome who also had Graves’ disease, discuss her management, and review the related literature. Pertinent published reports from 1950 through 2004 were researched with use of MEDLINE and PubMed, and cross-references to other articles were reviewed. Results: A 52-year-old white woman presented with symptoms of hyperthyroidism due to Graves’ disease. Laboratory data were as follows: thyrotropin <0.005 μIU/mL, thyroxine 11.1 μg/dL, free thyroxine index (FTI) 10.7, and triiodothyronine 170 ng/dL. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) and thyrotropin-binding inhibito- ry immunoglobulins (TBII) were positive at 1,986% and 82.5 U/L, respectively. The hyperthyroidism was treated with propranolol. She had a long-standing history of mus- culoskeletal complaints and was ultimately diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome. During her thyroid evalua- tion, she had severe neurologic deterioration that necessi- tated hospitalization and treatment with clonazepam, baclofen, intravenous immunoglobulin, and subsequently prednisone and azathioprine for appreciable symptomatic relief. The aggressive immunosuppression had a profound effect on her symptoms of hyperthyroidism, results of thy- roid function tests, and thyrotropin receptor antibodies (TRABs). Thyrotropin was 0.52 μIU/mL, thyroxine was 6.9 μg/dL, and FTI was 5.7. The TSI decreased from 1,986% to 248%, and her TBII normalized from 82.5 U/L to <5 U/L. She was clinically and biochemically euthyroid at last follow-up in May 2004. Conclusion: This case illustrates the association between TRAB-positive Graves’ disease and stiff-person syndrome and the improvement of Graves’ disease with immunosuppressive therapy. (Endocr Pract. 2005;11: 259-264) INTRODUCTION Graves’ disease is a common autoimmune disorder with an annual incidence of 80 cases per 100,000 in women and 10 cases per 100,000 in men (1,2). The iden- tification of the long-acting thyroid stimulator (LATS) thyrotropin receptor as the target of the LATS IgG and demonstration of the presence of thyrotropin receptor anti- bodies (TRABs) in more than 95% of patients with Graves’ disease indicate an autoimmune basis. The strongest direct evidence comes from the stimulation of thyroid cellular activity in vitro by IgG from patients with Graves’ disease and the passive transfer of transient hyperthyroidism to the newborn of an affected pregnant mother (1,2). Graves’ disease is associated with many organ-specific autoimmune conditions, including type 1 diabetes mellitus, Addison’s disease, vitiligo, pernicious anemia, myasthenia gravis, and premature ovarian failure (2,3), as well as autoimmune antibody positivity even in the absence of overt clinical disease (4-7). Stiff-person (stiff-man) syndrome (SPS) is a rare neu- rologic syndrome of unknown cause, characterized by progressive painful muscle spasms, muscle stiffness, and muscle rigidity (8,9). SPS is a clinical diagnosis, associat- ed with positive anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies and a suggestive electromyogram (EMG) (4,10-13). CASE REPORT A 52-year-old right-handed white woman presented to the endocrine clinic for evaluation of hyperthyroidism. She had a 9-month history of anxiety, rapid speech, dysp- nea on exertion, generalized weakness, and tremulousness. She had no local neck symptoms. She reported intermit- tent fatigue, mood swings, restless sleep, heat intolerance, and excessive sweating. She had also noticed palpitations and had irregular menses. Although her appetite had increased, she had maintained a stable weight. She had some eyelid swelling and minimal discomfort. A review of systems revealed considerable muscle aches and stiffness in the back and legs, gait difficulties, frequent falls, diffi- culty climbing stairs, and urinary incontinence. Her histo- ry revealed hypertension, osteoarthritis with cervical and lumbar spondylosis, cholecystectomy, and tubal ligation. She reported a strong family history of Graves’ disease (sister and first cousin). She was married and had 3 chil- dren. She denied alcohol or tobacco use. Her drug history included tolterodine (Detrol), sertraline (Zoloft), baclofen, and lisinopril. On physical examination, the patient’s weight was 82.1 kg, height was 165 cm, pulse was 84 beats/min, and blood pressure was 210/90 mm Hg. She looked anxious, with a stare, chemosis, and lid lag. The rest of the eye examination, including exophthalmometry, showed no other abnormalities. She had fine tremors of the out- stretched hands; normal findings on thyroid examination; brisk symmetric reflexes; proximal myopathy; abnormal gait, almost spastic in nature; and spasm of the anterior abdominal wall and paraspinal musculature. The rest of her examination was unremarkable. Initial thyroid function tests indicated biochemical hyperthyroidism (Table 1). Radioiodine ( 131I) thyroid uptake was 16% at 4 hours (estimated as 33% at 24 hours), and the scan showed a homogeneous pattern. TRABs were positive (Table 1). Thyrotropin-binding inhibitory immunoglobulins (TBII) were measured by radioreceptor assay (Kronus, Inc.), and thyroid-stimulating immuno- globulins (TSI) were measured by a cell bioassay, as described previously (16). Treatment with propranolol (40 mg three times daily) was initiated. Before her visit to the endocrine clinic, the patient had had several consultations with specialists, including a rheumatologist, spine orthopedist, pulmonologist, and neurologist. She had an extensive evaluation, including magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, which showed normal findings, and of the spine, which disclosed moder- ate cervical and lumbar spondylosis without spinal cord compromise. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Westergren), C-reactive protein, serum protein elec- trophoresis, and rheumatoid factor all demonstrated normal results. ty corrected for volume. Her EMG showed continuous activation of normal motor units of the paraspinal and proximal lower extremity muscles. The patient was diagnosed with SPS (elevated anti- GAD antibody level, 431 nmol/L; normal, ≤0.02 nmol/L). Treatment with baclofen yielded improvement in painful spasms, and she had no further falls. Her ambulation was substantially improved. Three months later, however, she required hospitalization because of worsening dyspnea, frequent falls, and increasing painful spasms. She was treated with clonazepam (Klonopin) but had little improvement. She received a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy (400 mg/kg daily). An echocardiogram showed normal findings, as did computed tomographic scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Subsequent improvement allowed her dismissal from the hospital. Within a month, deterioration of the patient’s condi- tion necessitated another 5-day course of IVIG, which yielded no improvement. She was then treated with a 5-day intravenous course of methylprednisolone at 1 g/day, and dramatic improvement ensued. She continued with orally administered prednisone in dosages up to 80 mg daily. Azathioprine (Imuran) (50 mg three times a day) was subsequently added because of a waning response to prednisone. Repeated performance of a radioiodine ( 131I) thyroid uptake and scan revealed essentially normal findings. Results of thyroid function tests were notably improved (Table 1). At follow-up, the patient was taking azathio- prine (150 mg/day) and prednisone (20 to 80 mg/day). She remained clinically euthyroid, with dramatically decreased symptoms of SPS. Incidentally, steroid-induced diabetes developed about 1 year after her initial endocrine evaluation, for which therapy with rosiglitazone (4 mg twice a day) was begun. Further evaluation revealed persistently positive anti- GAD antibodies (>100 U/mL; normal, <1.5 U/mL) 18 months after the initial evaluation. The TRABs were TSI 248% and TBII <5 U/L. The patient was positive for HLA-DQB1*0201/02 and 0201/02/03, HLA-DRB1*0301, HLA-DRB1*0701, HLA-DRB3*01, and HLA-DRB4*04 antigens.
